title: Separate actor identity, event classification and authority when adding speakers
summary: When a shared message path gains new kinds of speakers, replace human-only defaults with explicit speaker-aware classification and treat authority as separate evidence, not a property of speaker type.

conditions: A message or event path was originally written for one kind of speaker, often a human user.
The same path is later reused for agents, tools, services or other actor types.
The path contains hard-coded assumptions about the speaker, provenance, claim classification or authority.
problem_pattern.failure_mode: A new speaker is recorded using assumptions from the original human-only path. The event may retain a record of what was said while misrepresenting who said it, how it entered the system, what kind of claim it was, or whether authority was established.

generalised_method.action: List the actor types that the receiving integration actually supports. Distinguish message speakers from other participants or processes that never use this write path.

Trace the specific write path and list the attribution fields it really persists, such as actor identity, provenance/source, claim or inference kind, truth status, event type and authority. Do not assume every system has the same fields.
Resolve the actor from the receiving host's trusted identity assertion. A roster, participant type or local fixture key can help map an identity, but does not authenticate the person or agent.

Replace implicit human-only defaults with explicit rules for each supported speaker type. Use transport or source metadata where available; do not let a type label substitute for evidence about how an event entered the system.

Derive authority separately from authenticated permissions or explicit delegation evidence. Do not infer authority from human/agent type, membership, role, provenance label or ability to send a message. When the host supplies no authority evidence, record it as absent, unknown or unverified rather than inventing it.

Keep the acting agent or service distinct from any principal it claims to represent. Record an on-behalf-of relationship only if the host supplies evidence for that relationship and the receiving system has a field for it.

Exercise each supported speaker type through the actual write path. Assert correct actor and source classification, and negative cases such as an agent event acquiring human direct-user authority. Test unsupported or unknown speakers' fallback behaviour too.

Retest established human behaviour and compatibility after changing the shared mapping. Document any human-specific default that remains as a host- or fixture-specific assumption, not a universal rule.

applicability: Multi-agent applications adding agents to an existing human-facing message or event API.
Event-recording systems where multiple actor types share one write path.
Tool-using assistants that need to distinguish human messages, assistant messages and tool outputs.
Systems that record actions performed by an agent or service on behalf of another principal.
limitations: The originating AEL change was in a deterministic fixture runner, not a production host adapter or the core ledger append boundary.
The fixture resolves a speaker through its synthetic participant roster; it does not authenticate the speaker.

The fixture maps human messages to user_direct as a simulation convention. That value is not evidence of authentication, permission or real-world authorisation and must not be copied as a default into another system.
The PR #35 scenario tests human and agent attribution. Although the fixture code contains service, system and unknown branches, that PR's scenario does not independently exercise all of them.
The method does not define a permission system or prove that an agent was authorised to act for a principal.
Provenance labels and event records alone do not establish that a human saw, understood or approved an event.
This candidate is derived from one real repository correction and has not yet been adopted or evaluated by an independent receiving team.

checks: The pre-change fixture message path applied user provenance, direct-user authority and user-statement classification to every speaker.
The PR #35 correction selected an explicit mapping from the registered fixture participant type and preserved distinct agent actor identities.
The multi-agent fixture asserts separate human and agent message attribution; agent messages use assistant provenance and no human direct-user authority.
The same fixture records human branch decisions separately from agent proposals and messages.
The PR #35 CI run passed 88 tests on Python 3.11, 3.12 and 3.13.
A scope review narrowed the generalisation to what the fixture code and tests demonstrate, and separated fixture authority conventions from transferable advice.
not_established: Authentication behaviour in a live hosted chat or multi-agent platform.
Actual permission or delegation checks for human or agent actions.
Tested behaviour for every service, system and unknown-speaker branch.
Correctness of every receiving system's provenance or authority mapping.
External-team usefulness or adoption of this skill.

provenance.source_scope: Deterministic fixture runner and its integration scenario; not the production host adapter or core ledger append boundary.

reuse_guidance: Use as a review aid when adding actor types to a shared message or event path. First identify what the receiving system actually records and how it authenticates speakers. Map actor identity and event source explicitly; establish authority separately from trusted host evidence. Do not copy the AEL fixture's human user_direct default as an authorisation rule.
